result: Field experiments revealed complementary patterns of reproductive success between burying beetles and blowflies across temperature gradients. Beetle reproductive success peaked at intermediate temperatures while blowfly success was highest at temperature extremes (low and high).
evaluation: Claims C66 and C67 are directly supported by field data shown in Figure 1A-B with statistical analysis (Supplementary file 1a). The complementary temperature-dependent patterns are clearly demonstrated with appropriate sample sizes and statistical testing.

result: In field conditions, mites act as density-dependent and temperature-dependent protective mutualists. At 10 mites, there was little effect on beetle success but significant reduction in blowfly success at temperature extremes. At 20 mites, beetles showed enhanced reproductive success specifically at lower and higher temperatures, with corresponding declines in blowfly success. Mite reproductive success was not explained by temperature alone.
evaluation: Claims C68-C75 are well-supported by field experimental data (Figure 1C-F, Supplementary file 1a). The density-dependent and temperature-dependent effects are demonstrated with appropriate statistical analyses. The conclusion that mites act as protective mutualists is justified by the data showing enhanced beetle fitness when blowflies are present, particularly at temperature extremes with high mite densities.

result: Laboratory experiments confirmed that blowflies reduce beetle reproductive success in a temperature-dependent manner, with greater reduction at higher temperatures. Conversely, beetles substantially reduce blowfly success, with the strongest effect at intermediate temperatures and weaker effects at temperature extremes.
evaluation: Claims C76-C79 are supported by Laboratory Experiment 1 data with appropriate statistical tests (χ² tests, post-hoc comparisons with reported p-values). The reciprocal competitive effects and their temperature dependence are clearly demonstrated through controlled laboratory conditions.

result: Blowflies negatively impact mite reproductive success in a temperature-dependent manner. Mites experienced fitness loss at mid and higher temperatures but not at lower temperatures when blowflies were present.
evaluation: Claims C80-C84 are supported by Laboratory Experiment 1 data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1b) with appropriate statistical analyses including post-hoc comparisons. The temperature-dependent modulation of blowfly effects on mite fitness is clearly demonstrated.

result: In the absence of blowflies, mites have density-dependent negative effects on beetle fitness. Groups of 10 mites had no significant effect, while 20 mites significantly reduced beetle reproductive success. However, the harm caused by mites was substantially less than that caused by blowflies.
evaluation: Claims C85-C89 are supported by Laboratory Experiment 1 data (Figure 2A-C, Supplementary file 1b) with appropriate statistical tests. The density-dependent effects are clearly demonstrated, and the comparison with blowfly effects provides important context. The conclusion aligns with previous literature (cited appropriately).

result: Mites switch from harmful to mutualistic when blowflies are present, with effects dependent on both temperature and mite density. At lower temperatures, neither mite density affected beetle success. At higher temperatures, only 20 mites significantly increased beetle reproductive success, with corresponding declines in blowfly success.
evaluation: Claims C90-C95 are well-supported by Laboratory Experiment 1 data (Figures 2D-F, Figure 3, Supplementary file 1b) with comprehensive statistical analyses. The context-dependent switch from antagonism to mutualism is clearly demonstrated through controlled manipulations of blowfly presence, temperature, and mite density.

result: Beetles can defend against blowflies at intermediate temperatures but struggle at temperature extremes. Without mites, blowflies had highest success at temperature extremes. Adding 10 mites did not significantly reduce blowfly larvae, but 20 mites caused blowflies to perform poorly at all temperatures.
evaluation: Claims C96-C100 are supported by combined field and laboratory data (Figures 1B, 2D, 3A-C) with appropriate statistical analyses. The temperature-dependent effectiveness of beetle defenses and the density-dependent effects of mites on blowfly success are clearly demonstrated.

result: Temperature did not explain variation in blowfly reproductive success or carcass consumption rate when beetles were absent. However, blowfly development was greatly accelerated at higher temperatures, with significantly reduced time spent as eggs and 1st instar larvae.
evaluation: Claims C106-C110 are supported by Laboratory Experiment 2 data (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1c) with appropriate statistical tests. The distinction between developmental rate (temperature-dependent) and overall reproductive success (not temperature-dependent) is clearly demonstrated.

result: Beetle carcass preparation reduces blowfly success in a temperature-dependent manner. Beetles produced rounder carcasses at higher and mid temperatures compared to lower temperatures, and rounder carcasses were associated with fewer surviving blowfly larvae. The greatest blowfly fitness loss occurred at intermediate temperatures.
evaluation: Claims C111-C115 are supported by Laboratory Experiments 2 and 3 data (Figure 4B-C, Supplementary file 1d) with appropriate statistical analyses. The mechanistic link between carcass roundness and blowfly survival is demonstrated through correlation analysis (χ² = 13.78, p<0.001).

result: The combined effects of temperature on beetle carcass preparation and blowfly development explain why blowflies pose greater threats at temperature extremes. At intermediate temperatures, beetles defend effectively through carcass preparation. At higher temperatures, rapid blowfly development allows evasion of beetle defenses. At lower temperatures, beetle defenses are less effective.
evaluation: Claims C116-C120 represent integrative conclusions supported by multiple experimental results (Laboratory Experiments 1-3). The mechanistic explanation linking temperature effects on both beetle behavior and blowfly development is well-supported by the data, though some aspects involve inference from the combined results.

result: The beetle-mite interaction depends on blowfly presence, with mite predation on blowfly eggs indirectly enhancing beetle fitness. The extent of mutualism varies with temperature stress and mite density, with all three factors determining whether mites harm or help beetles.
evaluation: Claims C121-C125 are supported by the combined field and laboratory experimental results. The context-dependent nature of the interaction is clearly demonstrated through systematic manipulation of blowfly presence, temperature, and mite density. Figure 5 effectively summarizes these complex interactions.

result: Mites were antagonistic to beetles at all temperatures when blowflies were absent, consistent with previous work. Similar patterns have been observed in other protective mutualisms when enemy species are removed, often with hosts reducing rewards to mutualists.
evaluation: Claims C126-C128 are supported by Figure 2 data and appropriately cited literature (Wilson, 1983; Hopkins et al., 2017; Palmer et al., 2015, 2008). The comparison to other protective mutualisms provides valuable context for interpreting the results.

result: It remains unclear whether beetles modulate rewards to mites based on blowfly presence. The main service beetles provide is transport, making it difficult to modulate this service in response to local blowfly prevalence. Other mite species or nematodes might modulate P. carabi effects, but this requires future investigation.
evaluation: Claims C129-C133 represent speculation and identify gaps in knowledge rather than presenting supported findings. While the reasoning is logical, these claims explicitly acknowledge uncertainty and call for future work. No data are presented to test these hypotheses.

result: Unlike some protective mutualisms that break down at high temperatures due to mutualist vulnerability, mites showed no increased vulnerability to temperature. Instead, the main driver of change in the mutualism came from temperature effects on blowflies and beetle behavior.
evaluation: Claims C134-C137 are supported by the experimental data showing no direct temperature effects on mite fitness (C72, C136) combined with clear temperature effects on blowflies and beetles (Figure 4). The comparison to other mutualisms is appropriately cited (Chamberlain et al., 2014; Barton and Ives, 2014; etc.).

result: Similar effects might be found in other protective mutualisms where enemies thrive at high temperatures, provided both partners tolerate thermal stress. Predicting population responses to temperature variation requires understanding ecological community interactions and thermal tolerance of mutualistic partners.
evaluation: Claims C138-C139 represent speculation about broader implications and generalizability. While the reasoning is sound and appropriately cited (Early and Keith, 2019), these are hypotheses for future testing rather than demonstrated findings from this study.

result: Mite defense capacity was both temperature-dependent and density-dependent, with high mite densities needed to neutralize blowfly threats at higher temperatures. The experiments captured natural variation in mite density, but there is no evidence beetles can regulate mite density in anticipation of threats.
evaluation: Claims C140-C144 are supported by the combined field and laboratory data. The density-dependence and temperature-dependence are clearly demonstrated. The statement about natural mite density variation is supported by field observations (C149-C150), and the lack of beetle regulation is appropriately cited (Sun et al., 2019).

result: The protective mutualism between beetles and P. carabi mites is context-dependent, depending on complex interplay of biotic and abiotic factors. Short-term variation in mutualism expression may influence beetle persistence in adverse environments.
evaluation: Claim C145 is well-supported as the main conclusion synthesizing all experimental results. Claim C146 is more speculative about broader ecological implications, appropriately cited (Afkhami et al., 2014; Johnson, 2015; Peay, 2016), but represents a reasonable inference from the demonstrated context-dependence.

result: Temperature stress modulates harm from blowflies and induces mites to become protective mutualists. Mites compete with beetle larvae and reduce beetle success without blowflies, but enhance beetle success by eating blowfly eggs when blowflies are present. High mite densities are especially effective at temperature extremes when blowflies are more potent rivals.
evaluation: Claims C3-C9 represent the core findings stated in the abstract and are comprehensively supported by the field and laboratory experimental data. The temperature-dependent, density-dependent, and context-dependent (blowfly presence) nature of the mutualism is clearly demonstrated through systematic manipulations and appropriate statistical analyses.

result: Field experiments were conducted at Madingley Woods, an ancient woodland in Cambridgeshire, UK. Beetles discovered baited traps in a mean of 3.42 ± 0.77 days. Field-caught beetles naturally carried a mean of 10.82 ± 0.45 mites, with 70% carrying 1-20 mites.
evaluation: Claims C147-C150 describe methodological details and observational data that are clearly reported with appropriate descriptive statistics. The site description is appropriately cited (Goldberg et al., 2007), and the mite density data provide important context for the experimental manipulations.

result: While ecological conditions are known to change mutualism expression, the causal agents remain poorly understood. Contextual factors driving variation on ecological timescales are less well understood, especially for protective mutualisms. It is unclear how biotic and abiotic factors combine to influence mutualism expression, whether mutualisms are density-dependent, and how temperature, mite density, and blowflies interact to determine beetle-mite interactions.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C15-C17, and C65 accurately characterize gaps in knowledge that motivate the study. These are appropriately cited (Chamberlain et al., 2014; Hoeksema and Bruna, 2015; Hopkins et al., 2017; Palmer et al., 2015) and establish the rationale for the research questions addressed.
